summary: Sets out conventions for digitally signing Internet-Drafts. It uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax to make a detached signature stored in a separate companion file, so existing tools that handle drafts keep working unchanged.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5485 defines a separate digital-signature file for an Internet-Draft. A reader can verify the signature to check whether the draft's contents match the signed version.

subtitle: How the IETF Secretariat signs Internet-Drafts without changing the draft file.

tldr.problem: A person with an Internet-Draft needs a way to check that it matches the version posted by the IETF Secretariat without changing the file format used by existing tools.
tldr.mechanism: The Secretariat creates a detached Cryptographic Message Syntax signature and posts it in a separate companion file after canonicalizing text files.
tldr.outcome: The signature helps confirm that the draft has not changed since posting. The RFC is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8358.

today: RFC 5485 is Informational and was updated by RFC 8358. It has not been obsoleted according to the batch metadata.

sections.title: A Separate Signature File
sections.content:
The IETF Secretariat creates a detached Cryptographic Message Syntax signature for an Internet-Draft and posts it as a companion file. The signature is separate so it does not affect utilities that already process the draft.

The signature is intended to let anyone check that the contents have not changed since the Secretariat posted them. The signing-time records the Secretariat's wall-clock time; it is not a trusted timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature is stored separately from the draft. A successful check shows that the draft content matches what the Secretariat signed.

sections.title: File Names and Canonicalization
sections.content:
The signature file uses the same name as the draft with .p7s added. The two files can be stored anywhere; their names link them.

Plain-text drafts are canonicalized before signing so that different line-ending conventions do not change the signed data. The rules use 8-bit NVT-ASCII, CRLF line endings, no trailing spaces and no trailing blank lines. XML line endings are converted to LF; other formats are treated as octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Before signing a text draft, implementations use the same line-ending and whitespace rules. This lets different systems check the same signature against the same content.

sections.title: The CMS Signature Profile
sections.content:
The signature file contains a CMS ContentInfo holding SignedData. Since the signature is detached, the draft itself is not stored inside SignedData and the eContent field is absent.

The Secretariat includes signed content-type, message-digest and signing-time attributes. The profile uses version 3 for SignedData and SignerInfo. The certificate needed to verify the signature should be included.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature file contains the signature and information needed to check it, but not another copy of the draft. It records the content type, a digest of the draft and the signing time.

sections.title: Protecting the Signing Key
sections.content:
The Secretariat must protect its private signing key. The RFC strongly recommends a hardware security module because anyone who compromises the key could create signatures that appear to come from the Secretariat.

The signing system relies on good random-number generation for key creation, and it should be possible to change cryptographic algorithms as they weaken over time. Batch signing can keep the hardware module offline except when signatures are made.
sections.plainLanguage: The private key must be kept secure because it can create signatures trusted as the Secretariat's. The signing process also needs strong random values and a way to change algorithms over time.

sections.title: Why the Signature Is Detached
sections.content:
The RFC uses detached signatures for every draft file format, including formats that have their own signature methods. One method simplifies the Secretariat's work and does not interfere with signatures an author may already include.

Using file names to link the draft and signature lets both files be copied or stored outside the IETF repository and still be checked. The appendix gives an OpenSSL command as an example of verification.
sections.plainLanguage: The separate signature file keeps the draft unchanged and can travel with it to another location. A verifier needs the canonicalized draft, the signature file and a trusted certificate.
